title: Smart Pointers
summary: Smart pointers are RAII wrappers that delete a heap object automatically. `std::unique_ptr` has **one owner** and is the default. `std::shared_ptr` shares ownership by counting references. `std::weak_ptr` observes without owning. Create them with `std::make_unique` and `std::make_shared`.
markdown:
## Ownership, in the type [[7.02 new and delete — Dynamic Memory]] ended on a problem: a raw pointer cannot say who is responsible for deleting. A **smart pointer** is a small class that owns a heap object and deletes it in its destructor. It is RAII for `new`. ```mermaid flowchart TD Q{"Is a heap object
needed at all?"} -- no --> S["Use a plain value
or a std::vector"] Q -- yes --> O{"How many owners?"} O -- "exactly one" --> U["std::unique_ptr
(the default)"] O -- "several, and no clear last one" --> SH["std::shared_ptr"] SH --> C{"Could the owners
form a cycle?"} C -- yes --> W["Break it with std::weak_ptr"] ``` All three live in ``. ## `std::unique_ptr`: one owner ```cpp #include #include #include struct Player { std::string name{}; int hp{ 100 }; }; int main() { auto hero{ std::make_unique("Aria", 100) }; hero->hp -= 10; std::cout << hero->name << ' ' << hero->hp << '\n'; return 0; } // the Player is deleted here, automatically ``` ``` hero (unique_ptr) ──owns──▶ [ Player "Aria" ] hero goes out of scope: its destructor deletes the Player ``` | Property | Detail | |---|---| | Use | Like a pointer: `*p`, `p->member`, `if (p)` | | Cost | The same size and speed as a raw pointer | | Copying | Not allowed: two owners would both delete | | Moving | Allowed: ownership is transferred | ```cpp auto a{ std::make_unique(5) }; auto b{ std::move(a) }; // b now owns the int; a is null if (!a) { std::cout << "a is empty\n"; } ``` `std::make_unique(arguments)` allocates and constructs in one step and returns the `unique_ptr`. There is no `new` in your code and no `delete` anywhere. ### Passing smart pointers to functions This is where people go wrong. Most functions should not mention the smart pointer at all. | The function wants to | Parameter type | Call | |---|---|---| | Use the object | `Player&` or `const Player&` | `heal(*hero);` | | Use it, and it may be absent | `Player*` | `inspect(hero.get());` | | Take over ownership | `std::unique_ptr` by value | `adopt(std::move(hero));` | A function that only uses a `Player` has no business knowing how its caller stores it. Taking a reference keeps it usable with objects on the stack too. ## `std::shared_ptr`: shared ownership Sometimes an object has several owners and no way to know which will finish with it last. A `shared_ptr` keeps a **reference count** of its owners and deletes the object when the count reaches zero. ```cpp auto texture{ std::make_shared("grass.png") }; // count is 1 { auto alias{ texture }; // count is 2 std::cout << texture.use_count() << '\n'; // 2 } // count is 1 // when the last owner goes, the Texture is deleted ``` ``` sprite1 ─┐ sprite2 ─┼──▶ [ control block: count 3 ] ──▶ [ Texture ] sprite3 ─┘ each copy adds 1, each destruction subtracts 1, and at 0 the object is deleted ``` It is not free: there is a separate **control block** holding the count, and updating the count must be safe across threads. Use it only when ownership really is shared. If one clear owner exists, use `unique_ptr` and give everyone else a reference. ## Cycles and `std::weak_ptr` Reference counting has one failure mode. ```cpp struct Person { std::string name{}; std::shared_ptr partner{}; }; auto ann{ std::make_shared("Ann") }; auto bob{ std::make_shared("Bob") }; ann->partner = bob; bob->partner = ann; // ann and bob go out of scope: each count drops to 1, never to 0. Both leak. ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Ann (count 1)"] -->|shared_ptr| B["Bob (count 1)"] B -->|shared_ptr| A ``` Each keeps the other alive for ever. The fix is for one direction not to own. A `std::weak_ptr` refers to an object managed by `shared_ptr` **without** adding to the count. ```cpp struct Person { std::string name{}; std::weak_ptr partner{}; }; if (auto p{ ann->partner.lock() }) { std::cout << p->name << '\n'; } ``` A `weak_ptr` cannot be dereferenced directly, because the object might already be gone. `lock()` returns a `shared_ptr` that is either valid or empty, so the check and the access cannot be separated. The usual shape: a parent owns its children, and each child refers back to its parent with a `weak_ptr` or a plain pointer. ## Summary | | `unique_ptr` | `shared_ptr` | `weak_ptr` | Raw `T*` | |---|---|---|---|---| | Owns the object | Yes, alone | Yes, jointly | No | No, by convention | | Can be copied | No, only moved | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Overhead | None | A control block and counting | Small | None | | Deletes automatically | Yes | When the count reaches 0 | | No | > [!tip] The modern rules > - Do not write `new` or `delete` in ordinary code. Use `std::make_unique` and `std::make_shared`. > - Raw pointers and references are fine, as **non-owning** observers. > - Default to `unique_ptr`. Reach for `shared_ptr` only when you can explain why there are several owners. A `unique_ptr` can also manage things other than memory, by giving it a function to call in place of `delete`. That function is a **custom deleter**: ```cpp std::unique_ptr file{ std::fopen("data.txt", "r"), &std::fclose }; ``` ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Why can a `unique_ptr` not be copied? + A copy would create two owners of the same object, and both would delete it - Because it is stored on the heap - Because it has no copy constructor by accident - Because copying a pointer is undefined behaviour > `unique_ptr` means one owner. Ownership can be handed over with `std::move`, but not duplicated. ? How does `weak_ptr` break a cycle? - It deletes one of the objects in the cycle + It does not add to the reference count, so the counts can still reach zero - It makes the `shared_ptr`s unique - It copies the objects so they no longer refer to each other > Two `shared_ptr`s pointing at each other keep both counts above zero forever. A `weak_ptr` observes without owning. ? What should a function that only reads a `Player` take? - `std::shared_ptr` - `std::unique_ptr` + `const Player&` - `Player*` it must delete > A function that only uses an object should not care how it is owned. Pass smart pointers only when ownership is part of the job. ? When is `shared_ptr` the right choice? - Whenever you allocate on the heap - When you want the fastest smart pointer - When the object has one clear owner + When several owners share it and none is clearly last > `shared_ptr` costs a reference count. Use `unique_ptr` by default and `shared_ptr` only for truly shared ownership. ```
ideas:
1. Replace every `new` and `delete` in your earlier Milestone 7 code with `unique_ptr`.
2. Build a parent and child tree with `shared_ptr` children and `weak_ptr` parents, and print the `use_count` values.
3. Create a cycle and show that it leaks (the destructor never prints). Then fix it with `weak_ptr`.

cards.q: Why can a `unique_ptr` not be copied?
cards.a:
A copy would create two owners of the same object, and both would delete it

`unique_ptr` means one owner. Ownership can be handed over with `std::move`, but not duplicated.

It does not add to the reference count, so the counts can still reach zero

Two `shared_ptr`s pointing at each other keep both counts above zero forever. A `weak_ptr` observes without owning.

cards.q: What should a function that only reads a `Player` take?
cards.a:
`const Player&`

A function that only uses an object should not care how it is owned. Pass smart pointers only when ownership is part of the job.

When several owners share it and none is clearly last

`shared_ptr` costs a reference count. Use `unique_ptr` by default and `shared_ptr` only for truly shared ownership.
